summary: Hebrew has no verb “to have”. It says that the thing exists “to” the owner: יֵשׁ “there is” + לְ “to” + the owner — יֵשׁ לִי אָח “I have a brother”, literally “there is to me a brother”. With a pronoun, לְ takes the personal endings: לִי, לְךָ (to a man), לָךְ (to a woman), לוֹ, לָהּ, לָנוּ, לָכֶם, לָכֶן, לָהֶם, לָהֶן. יֵשׁ itself never changes. Because the thing owned is the grammatical subject, the past and the future use הָיָה agreeing with that thing — not with the owner: הָיָה לִי מַפְתֵּחַ, הָיְתָה לִי דִּירָה, הָיוּ לִי סְפָרִים; יִהְיֶה לָנוּ תִּינוֹק, תִּהְיֶה לָהֶם תִּינֹקֶת. The negative replaces יֵשׁ with אֵין (אֵין לִי …, lesson 8).

blocks.caption: In the past and future הָיָה agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner.

blocks.title: Having = existing for someone
blocks.text: The thing owned is the subject of the sentence. That is why הָיָה agrees with it, and why standard Hebrew puts no אֶת before it even when it is definite: יֵשׁ לִי הַסֵּפֶר (in speech יֵשׁ לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר is very common).

blocks.title: No “I have” verb
blocks.text: *אֲנִי יֵשׁ אָח is wrong: the owner is never the subject. Say יֵשׁ לִי אָח — or, to stress the owner, לִי יֵשׁ אָח.

blocks.title: Have ≠ my
blocks.text: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר “I have a book” — הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי “my book”. לְ is for having, שֶׁל for belonging.

blocks.title: The negative is a different word
blocks.text: Not *לֹא יֵשׁ, but אֵין: אֵין לִי אַחִים “I have no brothers” (lesson 8).

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Who is the owner? (→ לִי, לוֹ, לָהּ …)
In the past or future: what gender and number has the thing owned?

askYourself: Who is the owner? → the form of לְ: לִי, לְךָ / לָךְ, לוֹ, לָהּ, לָנוּ, לָכֶם / לָכֶן, לָהֶם / לָהֶן.
Am I speaking to a man or to a woman? → לְךָ or לָךְ.
Is it now? → יֵשׁ, which never changes.
Is it past or future? → הָיָה / הָיְתָה / הָיוּ or יִהְיֶה / תִּהְיֶה / יִהְיוּ, agreeing with the THING owned (its gender and number).
Is the thing definite? → standard Hebrew adds no אֶת.
Is it negative? → אֵין instead of יֵשׁ (lesson 8).
steps: Put יֵשׁ (or the agreeing form of הָיָה) in front.

traps: *אֲנִי יֵשׁ אָח — the owner goes into לְ: יֵשׁ לִי אָח.
*הָיִיתִי לִי אָחוֹת — the past agrees with the thing, not the owner: הָיְתָה לִי אָחוֹת.
*הָיָה לִי שְׁנֵי טֶלֶפוֹנִים — two phones are plural: הָיוּ לִי שְׁנֵי טֶלֶפוֹנִים.
לְךָ is to a man, לָךְ to a woman: יֵשׁ לְךָ? / יֵשׁ לָךְ?
*לֹא יֵשׁ — the negative is אֵין לִי.
יֵשׁ לִי ≠ שֶׁלִּי: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר “I have a book”, הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי “my book”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has no verb “have” either: عِنْدِي أَخ / لِي أَخ — a preposition with the owner’s suffix, like לִי, but without a word for “there is”.
German uses the verb haben with an accusative object (ich habe einen Bruder); in Hebrew the thing owned is the subject.
Chinese uses the verb 有 (我有一个哥哥) — the same word as “there is”, just as Hebrew יֵשׁ means both.

notes.text: у меня есть брат “at me there is a brother” is the same idea as יֵשׁ לִי אָח “there is to me a brother”: no verb “have”. Hebrew uses “to” (לְ) where Russian uses “at” (у), and in both the past agrees with the thing owned: у меня была сестра ~ הָיְתָה לִי אָחוֹת.

Turkish says “my brother exists” (kardeşim var); Hebrew says “there is to me a brother” (יֵשׁ לִי אָח). The negative is a word of its own in both: yok ~ אֵין. Turkish abi / ağabey and kardeş are all אָח: Hebrew does not split siblings by age.
Greek has a verb, έχω; Hebrew has none — it says יֵשׁ לִי “there is to me”. Do not look for a verb to conjugate: only לְ changes for the owner.
Spanish tener has no Hebrew counterpart: “I have” is יֵשׁ לִי “there is to me”. The owner goes into לְ, and only לְ changes (לִי, לְךָ, לָהּ …).
English “have” is a verb; Hebrew uses “there is” + “to me”: יֵשׁ לִי. In the past the verb agrees with the thing owned: הָיְתָה לִי דִּירָה “I had a flat” (literally “a flat was to me”).
French avoir has no counterpart: Hebrew says “there is to me”, יֵשׁ לִי — close to il y a. The past agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.
German haben (ich habe einen Bruder) has no Hebrew counterpart; the thing owned is the subject and the owner is in לְ: יֵשׁ לִי אָח.
Hindi also has no “have” verb: मेरे पास किताब है “near me is a book”, and मेरा एक भाई है for relatives; Hebrew has one construction for both: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר, יֵשׁ לִי אָח.
Persian has a verb, داشتن (کتاب دارم); Hebrew has none: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר.
Marathi says माझ्याकडे पुस्तक आहे “with me is a book” and मला भाऊ आहे “to me is a brother”; Hebrew uses one pattern for both: יֵשׁ לִי.
Arabic uses prepositions too (عِنْدِي كِتَابٌ, لِي أَخٌ) but no word like יֵשׁ; Hebrew always says יֵשׁ in the present and אֵין in the negative.
Japanese says “to me there is” (私には兄がいる); Hebrew is the same idea: יֵשׁ לִי אָח — with one word for people and things (no いる / ある split). 兄 and 弟 are both אָח: Hebrew does not split siblings by age.
Korean uses 있다 “exist” (저는 형이 있어요); Hebrew יֵשׁ is the same idea, with the owner in לְ: יֵשׁ לִי אָח. 형 / 오빠 and 남동생 are all אָח: no older / younger split.
Finnish minulla on veli “at me is a brother” is the same pattern as יֵשׁ לִי אָח; Hebrew uses “to” (לְ) where Finnish uses -lla. Negative: minulla ei ole ~ אֵין לִי.

Hungarian nekem van egy bátyám “to me there is a brother of mine” is close to יֵשׁ לִי אָח; the negative is a word of its own in both: nincs ~ אֵין. Báty and öcs are both אָח: Hebrew does not split brothers by age.
Swahili says “I am with” (nina kitabu); Hebrew says “there is to me” (יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר) — the owner is in לְ, not in a verb prefix.
Luganda says “I am with” (nnina ekitabo); Hebrew says “there is to me”: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר.

有 is both “have” and “there is” (我有一个哥哥 / 这儿有书); Hebrew יֵשׁ is both too, but the owner must be marked with לְ: יֵשׁ לִי — “there is to me”. And 哥哥 and 弟弟 are both אָח: Hebrew does not split siblings by age.
Vietnamese có is both “have” and “there is” (tôi có sách); Hebrew יֵשׁ is the same word for both, with the owner in לְ: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר. Anh trai and em trai are both אָח.
Inuktitut adds a “have” suffix (-qaq-) to the noun of the thing owned and makes it a verb; Hebrew uses separate words: יֵשׁ + לְ + the owner + the thing.
